prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which atoms trapped at a magic wavelength are probed without light-shift perturbation, opening a new regime of precision in the measurement of time and its use to test fundamental physics

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single-part prize for the optical lattice clock to Katori and Ye. After reading all eight statements, the position is stronger for me, not weaker, because the two objections raised against it are both about framing and neither is about the physics. The physics is a simple image. If the lattice wavelength is chosen so that the ground and clock states are shifted equally, the trap becomes invisible to the transition, and thousands of atoms can be held without Doppler or recoil broadening. Katori proposed that condition and pursued it in strontium; Ye's group took the neutral-atom clock to the stability and accuracy frontier, around 1e-18. What follows is the kind of result I look for: independent laboratories compare their clocks and agree, and the clocks then measure something new, namely gravitational redshift across millimetres, limits on drifts of constants and on ultralight dark matter, and a many-body description of the clock ensemble itself. As an atomic theorist who has computed the shifts that dominate such uncertainty budgets (blackbody radiation, higher-order light shifts), I can say the 1e-18 claims are plausible and have been cross-checked by comparison, not only by self-assessment. On the chair's question about distinctness: the 2005 prize rewarded the comb as a frequency ruler and the 2012 prize rewarded quantum control of single ions. The lattice clock is a different physical idea, cancelling a systematic by design for a large ensemble, and the citation should say so in its wording. I am also asked whether to treat this as discovery or invention. I think it is both: the magic-wavelength condition was a discovery of how to decouple an atom from its trap, and the clocks have since produced physics that no earlier clock could.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is still category and overlap: a committee that has twice honoured the precision-spectroscopy chain may feel this is a third step and an instrument milestone. I think that is answerable in the citation but I cannot claim it is settled; it is a matter of judgment. Second, the credit is not provably complete. Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley, Bloom and the JILA and SYRTE collaborators, as well as the ion-clock groups, made real contributions, and none of us has checked the first lattice-clock publications against the record. My own recollection is that the magic-wavelength proposal and first demonstration sit with Katori and the high-accuracy strontium clock with Ye, but I am working from memory, as several colleagues are, and an expert report should confirm it before the vote. Third, the redefinition of the SI second has not happened, so part of the impact is prospective. I regard that as a timing argument and not a scientific one, since the comparisons between clocks that justify the redefinition already exist.

responses.point: Olle prefers twisted bilayer graphene (B001), argues that it opens a field no earlier prize has touched and that its reproduction across moire platforms answers the question of stability, and notes that the optical lattice clock risks being the third step in a metrology chain after 2005 and 2012. He says he would be comfortable with B007 as a serious alternative.
responses.response: I accept the overlap concern as real, and I think we should answer it in the citation and not wave it away: the comb is a ruler, single-ion control is a different object, and the lattice clock is about trapping many neutral atoms with the trap's light shift cancelled. On B001 I agree that reproduction across platforms is strong evidence of a robust phenomenon, and the theory-then-experiment sequence is the kind of loop I admire. My remaining difficulty is not the existence of the phases but what we would be rewarding: the pairing mechanism is open, and you and Bernhard both concede that Cao and the first experimental authors, and earlier twisted-bilayer theory, sit outside the three names. I defer to you on the condensed-matter physics, and I would not oppose B001 if the expert reports resolve the credit question, but today the clock has the cleaner map from achievement to people. Your point that the two cases are not in conflict is fair, and it is why B001 is my first alternative.

responses.point: Bernhard prefers B001 because a simple analytical continuum model made a sharp prediction that was tested directly, argues that an unresolved pairing mechanism is not a maturity problem (cuprates are cited), and states that if the discovery is judged not settled enough, B007 is the more mature and less contested choice.
responses.response: The cuprate comparison is a good one and it moved me part of the way: an open mechanism has not stopped the committee honouring discoveries before, and I will not treat it as a reason in itself to refuse B001. What it does not remove is the credit fragility you also name, and I appreciate that you say so openly. Where I still differ is in the weight of the two risks. For B007 the main exposure is category and possible missing names, which a careful citation and an expert report can address. For B001 the exposure is that three names will be read as contestable by the community, and the youngest of the experiments is eight years old. Your own statement that B007 is the more mature and less contested fallback is close to the way I reason, and I take it as agreement that the two cases differ mainly in credit risk, not in scientific quality.

responses.point: Stefan supports B007 and, in reply to my first-round ranking, argues that the Cirac-Zoller proposal (B015) is theory-only, separated from the experimental realisations by Wineland, Blatt, Monroe and others, and recently adjacent to the 2022 and 2025 prizes, so he keeps it off his alternatives. He also flags his year in Hall's laboratory as a possible link to Ye.
responses.response: You are right about B015, and I have changed my view of it. A theory-only prize for the gate proposal would be separated from the experimental credit that made it matter, and the committee has recently rewarded adjacent quantum-information ground, so I now treat it as a weaker alternative than I did in round 1. I keep it as a second alternative only because it is atomic physics where I can judge the content, not because I think it is competitive this year. On your disclosure, I do not think having worked a year in the laboratory of Ye's former mentor is a conflict that would require recusal, since it is a generation removed from the work being credited, but that is for the chair to decide. I also agree with you that the lattice-clock credit is separable into identifiable steps, and I would answer the chair's question the same way: the committee need not reopen the ion-clock credit.

responses.point: Ulf prefers B007, calls the redefinition of the second a concrete measure of maturity, and concedes that the ion-clock community and contributors such as Lemonde, Ludlow and Hinkley could be argued for, while relying on recollection of the history.
responses.response: I agree on the maturity point and I would put it more simply: independent clocks have been compared against one another, and that is a stronger test than most candidates can offer. On credit I see it a little differently from the way I framed it in round 1. I resisted joint recognition with the ion-clock groups, and I still do, but I now think the honest answer to the chair's question is that neither of us can settle Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley and Bloom from memory. As Secretary you could ask the experts to establish three things: who first proposed and first demonstrated the magic-wavelength lattice clock, who first reached the 1e-18 level, and whether the early strontium contributions are genuinely separable. I would hold to two names unless that record shows one of these steps belongs to someone else, and I would not add names without that evidence.

uncertainties: Whether the historical record, once checked, supports exactly Katori and Ye, or shows that an early lattice-clock step belongs to Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley or Bloom. My memory of the priority history is not a substitute for the documents.
Whether the committee accepts the lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 and 2012 prizes and as a new capability that has produced physics, and not a third metrology prize.
Whether a prize before the redefinition of the SI second is slightly early; I judge it a timing matter and not a scientific one.

Whether the credit questions for B001 (Cao and the first experimental authors, earlier twisted-bilayer theory) can be resolved by the experts, in which case B001 could become the stronger prize for a later year or a competing choice this year.
I cannot judge the condensed-matter case for B001 as well as colleagues who work in the field.
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged from round 1. I am a long-time close collaborator of Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate) and have co-authored with the Lund and ETH attosecond groups. I also did atomic-structure theory used in storage-ring experiments. None of this involves Katori, Ye, MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero, Bistritzer, Cirac or Zoller as far as my profile shows, so I see no conflict that requires recusal. I do note my atomic physics proximity to B007 and B015, and I will defer to the chair if the committee judges that any link, for instance Kroll's connection through John Hall's laboratory, should be handled differently.
